# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by the extracellular deposition of misfolded amyloid fibrils within the myocardium. Once considered a rare and uniformly fatal disease, CA is now increasingly recognized as an underdiagnosed cause of heart failure, particularly heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [1]. The two predominant forms are light-chain (AL) amyloidosis, arising from a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia, and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis, which may be hereditary (ATTRv) or wild-type (ATTRwt) [2]. Advances in non-invasive imaging and the emergence of disease-modifying therapies have transformed the diagnostic and therapeutic landscape [3].

## Epidemiology and Pathophysiology

ATTRwt amyloidosis is predominantly a disease of older men and has been identified in up to 13% of patients hospitalized with HFpEF and in a substantial proportion of patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement for severe aortic stenosis [4,5]. AL amyloidosis has an estimated incidence of approximately 10 cases per million person-years [6]. The hereditary form is associated with more than 130 pathogenic TTR variants; the Val122Ile variant, carried by 3–4% of individuals of African ancestry, is a notable cause of late-onset cardiomyopathy [7].

The pathophysiology involves destabilization of the transthyretin tetramer, dissociation into monomers, and subsequent aggregation into amyloid fibrils [8]. In AL amyloidosis, circulating free light chains exert direct cardiotoxic effects in addition to fibril deposition, contributing to disproportionately rapid clinical deterioration [9]. Amyloid infiltration produces increased ventricular wall thickness, diastolic dysfunction, and ultimately restrictive physiology [10].

## Clinical Presentation

CA should be suspected in patients with unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy, HFpEF in older adults, low-voltage ECG despite increased wall thickness, and intolerance to standard heart failure therapies [11]. Extracardiac "red flags" are valuable diagnostic clues, including bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, spontaneous biceps tendon rupture, and autonomic dysfunction [12]. AL amyloidosis may additionally present with nephrotic-range proteinuria, periorbital purpura, and macroglossia [13]. Conduction system disease and atrial fibrillation are common, and atrial thrombus may occur even in sinus rhythm [14].

## Diagnosis

Echocardiography typically demonstrates increased wall thickness with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction, and longitudinal strain imaging reveals a characteristic apical-sparing ("cherry-on-top") pattern [15]. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging shows diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement and elevated native T1 and extracellular volume [16].

A major advance has been the use of bone-avid radiotracer scintigraphy (technetium-labeled pyrophosphate, DPD, or HMDP), which enables non-invasive diagnosis of ATTR-CA with high specificity when monoclonal protein is excluded [17]. The Perugini grading system quantifies myocardial uptake [18]. Crucially, all patients require screening for a monoclonal protein with serum and urine immunofixation and serum free light-chain assay, as a positive scintigraphy result in the presence of a paraprotein may still represent AL amyloidosis and warrants biopsy [19]. Endomyocardial biopsy with Congo red staining and amyloid typing by mass spectrometry remains the gold standard when uncertainty persists [20].

## Treatment

Management of AL amyloidosis targets the underlying plasma cell clone. Bortezomib-based regimens, and increasingly the addition of the anti-CD38 antibody daratumumab, have improved hematologic and organ responses [21,22]. Autologous stem cell transplantation benefits carefully selected patients [23].

For ATTR-CA, tafamidis, a transthyretin stabilizer, reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in the landmark ATTR-ACT trial and remains a cornerstone of therapy [24]. Newer agents targeting hepatic TTR production—the RNA interference therapeutics patisiran and vutrisiran, and the antisense oligonucleotide inotersen—have shown efficacy in hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy, with vutrisiran demonstrating cardiovascular benefit in the HELIOS-B trial [25,26]. Acoramidis, a high-affinity stabilizer, also reduced cardiovascular events in the ATTRibute-CM study [27].

Supportive heart failure management emphasizes cautious diuresis; neurohormonal antagonists are often poorly tolerated owing to fixed stroke volume and hypotension [28]. Anticoagulation is generally recommended for atrial fibrillation given high thromboembolic risk [14]. Selected patients may be candidates for heart transplantation [29].

## Prognosis and Conclusion

Prognosis depends on amyloid type and stage at diagnosis. Validated staging systems based on cardiac biomarkers (NT-proBNP and troponin) and, for AL, the difference in free light chains, predict survival and guide therapy [30]. Untreated AL-CA carries the poorest outlook, but early diagnosis and contemporary therapy have markedly improved outcomes across both subtypes. Heightened clinical suspicion, integration of non-invasive imaging, and timely initiation of disease-modifying treatment are now essential to improving survival in this once-overlooked disease.
